title: How Stories Make Us Feel: Toward an Embodied Narratology
extended_summary:
This paper examines the rise of “neurohumanism” and its implications for literary studies, arguing that recent neuroscience and cognitive science have reopened long-standing questions about human identity, empathy, agency, and embodiment. The authors situate their argument against earlier antihumanist and posthumanist critiques in the humanities, then propose that contemporary neuroscience offers concepts that can enrich, rather than reduce, literary interpretation.

The paper’s main intervention is a theoretical model of “Feeling of Body” (FoB), grounded in embodied simulation and mirror-neuron research. The authors argue that narrative engagement is not only a matter of cognitively inferring characters’ minds (Theory of Mind), but also of bodily resonance with actions, emotions, and sensations represented in texts. On this view, reading fiction can activate embodied processes that support empathy and intersubjective understanding.

The paper is not an empirical study of learners or classrooms; it is a conceptual and interdisciplinary essay drawing on neuroscience, philosophy, and literary theory. Its conclusions are that embodied cognition provides a better complement to cognitive literary theory than disembodied models of mind-reading alone, and that narrative theory should take bodily simulation and affective resonance seriously as mechanisms through which stories move readers.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical humanities/neuroscience essay, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It does not use a comparative design, K-12 sample, or outcome measurement relevant to educational effectiveness.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper offers conceptual arguments about embodied narratology, empathy, and neuroscience, but reports no measured educational impact. It does not evaluate AI tools, science instruction, or K-12 scientific reasoning outcomes.
